lessons.title: పదకొండు, ఇరవై — the same pattern, worn down one step further
lessons.gloss: 11-20 — additive "ten-echo" compounds for the teens; ఇరవై (20) most likely continues the SAME pan-Dravidian "two-tens" pattern as Kannada's ippattu, though worn down further and less transparent on the surface today

segments.text: You just watched Kannada's twenty split cleanly into "two" + "ten." Telugu most likely comes from the exact same pattern — but centuries of extra erosion have worn it past the point of being visible today.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart - పదకొండు–పందొమ్మిది — "ten" + digit

segments.text: Telugu's teens echo పది (padi, "ten") plus each digit — పదకొండు (padakoṇḍu, 11), పన్నెండు (panneṇḍu, 12), and onward through పందొమ్మిది (paṅdommidi, 19) — the same "digit + ten-echo" compounding Kannada builds.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart - ఇరవై — most likely the same "two-tens," just worn further

segments.text: ఇరవై (iravai, "twenty") most likely continues the same pan-Dravidian pattern as Kannada's ippattu — an old iru-/renḍu ("two") root fused with an old "ten" root — but here's the honest difference: centuries of sound change have worn iravai down far enough that it no longer visibly splits into "two" and "ten" on the surface, the way Kannada's ippattu still does today. Telugu's own word for "two," రెండు (renḍu), doesn't obviously show up inside iravai anymore — treat this as the most likely comparative-Dravidian account rather than a transparent, easily re-derivable compound.

segments.instruction: "iravai" — twenty, most likely the same "two-tens" idea as Kannada, just worn down further
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "iravai" — twenty, most likely the same "two-tens" idea as Kannada, just worn down further]

segments.text: How are Telugu's teens built? (పది (ten) + a digit, compounded.) Does ఇరవై visibly split into "two" + "ten" today, the way Kannada's ippattu does? (No — it most likely continues the same pan-Dravidian pattern, but erosion has worn away the visible split.) What's Telugu's word for "two"? (రెండు, renḍu.)

lessons.title: వాతావరణం (vātāvaraṇam) — "the covering of air," pure Sanskrit this time
lessons.gloss: weather/atmosphere — a PURE Sanskrit compound, unlike Kannada's Persian+Sanskrit hybrid: vata ("air/wind") + avarana ("covering")

segments.text: Kannada's weather word mixed a Persian loan with a Sanskrit one. Telugu's is different again — a single, unmixed Sanskrit compound.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart - వాతావరణం — vāta + āvaraṇa

segments.text: వాతావరణం (vātāvaraṇam) = "weather, atmosphere" — built entirely from Sanskrit:
వాత (vāta, "wind, air") — the same Sanskrit root behind వాయువు (vāyuvu, "wind," and the wind-god Vāyu).
ఆవరణ (āvaraṇa, "covering, layer, enclosure").

So vātāvaraṇam literally means "the covering of air" — the layer of air surrounding everything, i.e., the atmosphere/weather. Unlike Kannada's havāmāna (Persian hava + Sanskrit māna), both pieces here are Sanskrit — no Perso-Arabic loan involved at all.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: వర్షం పడుతోంది — "rain is falling"

segments.text: వర్షం పడుతోంది. — "It's raining." — literally "rain is falling." (varṣaṁ paḍutōndi.) — వర్షం (varṣaṁ, "rain") is the same Sanskrit root, varṣā, you'll see again in the Dravidian arc.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "varṣaṁ paḍutōndi" — it's raining, "rain is falling"]

segments.text: What are the two Sanskrit pieces of వాతావరణం (vātāvaraṇam), and what does the whole word literally mean? (వాత, "air," + ఆవరణ, "covering" — "the covering of air.") Is either piece a Persian/Arabic loan, like part of Kannada's word? (No — both pieces are Sanskrit.) What word does Telugu use for "rain"? (వర్షం, varṣaṁ.)

lessons.title: డ (ḍa) — one character, met inside words you already say
lessons.gloss: the single character డ — recognised inside words you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: డ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: ఉ — what does it do?
One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
డ — ḍa.
It is a consonant, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an a already in it. So it is not ḍ, it is ḍa.
You already say these, and every one of them has డ (ḍa) somewhere inside it:
మాట్లాడు māṭlāḍu — to speak.
ఉండు uṇḍu — to be, to stay, to live.
ఒకటి రెండు మూడు నాలుగు ఐదు okaṭi reṇḍu mūḍu nālugu aidu — one to five.
పదకొండు — ఇరవై padakoṇḍu — iravai — 11-20 — additive "ten-echo" compounds for the teens; ఇరవై.

blocks.title: Writing: డ — copy what you see

segments.text: Put your pen on డ (ḍa) and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
